Climate shock adds to the challenges and makes the conditions for sustained peace and safe return more difficult to achieve. Therefore, the Security Council must take climate and environmental challenges into account and focus on climate, peace, and security in conflict prevention and peacebuilding frameworks. UN agencies and their humanitarian workers must always have safe and unhindered access to those in need. As obvious as it may sound, unfortunately, we still have to remind today that ensuring humanitarian access is a legal obligation of every state under international law. In conclusion, I would like to emphasize that humanitarian aid alone will not create the conditions for a safe return home. The Security Council has the responsibility to address the structural causes of displacement, not just the humanitarian consequences. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Latvia for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of the United States.

Thank you, President, and thank you, High Commissioner, for your briefing. The United States remains committed to constructively contributing to efforts to achieve peace and end displacement by fostering the conditions for refugees to return home. For example, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, The United States brokered the Washington Accords, which allowed displaced refugees to return home. The parties must demonstrate a continued and earnest commitment to this political process. For Sudan, the United States continues to advocate for a humanitarian truce and calls on parties to protect civilians and negotiate in good faith. Humanitarian assistance must be able to reach those in need. We have also renewed our efforts towards a swift and durable end to the Russia-Ukraine war through ceasefire and negotiated settlement. We continue to support the return of all civilians, especially children, who have been displaced or forcibly transferred as a result of this conflict. We must not forget about the too-often overlooked displacement crises, including the reality facing the Sirawee refugees. There is a window of opportunity to end this protracted political dispute and give these refugees a chance at a dignified and free future. We call on all member states and stakeholders to join us in making this opportunity a reality. In all these cases, the United States firmly believes that deterring and ending displacement, rather than just managing it year after year, must be the goal. In FY 2025, the United States contributed more than $1.4 billion in humanitarian assistance to UNHCR, UNICEF, and IOM. These funds help to address refugee crises, internal displacement, and disasters around the world, including Sudan, DRC, and Ukraine. The United States has also additionally provided billions of dollars through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs pooled funds, most of which supports the UNHCR activities. The international system, though, cannot continue to treat forced displacement as a burden for only host and donor states. Origin country actors must finally face accountability. Responsibility for these problems cannot continue to be quietly transferred to the rest of the world. Governments and countries of origin have a part to play, and we must hold them accountable and to a higher standard. They must create conditions for returns and promptly accept their returned nationals. We also believe that the UNHCR has a key role to play in fostering refugee returns. The United States supports the High Commissioner's 50 by 35 vision, where it reflects a genuine pivot towards solutions and self-reliance. We urge UNHCR to remain at the forefront of these worldwide efforts to support refugees so that they may finally return home. The global refugee and asylum system, however, cannot be sustained without significant reforms. UNHCR's most urgent priority should be to advance changes that halt the abuse of asylum mechanisms by economic migrants, perhaps the most powerful driver of mass migration. We look forward to the long overdue reforms to uphold national sovereignty and eliminate incentives for fraudulent abuses of the international protection system. Thank you.

I thank the representative of the United States. For that statement, I will now deliver a statement in my capacity as the representative of France. I thank Mr. Baham Sali, the High Commissioner for Refugees, for his first briefing to the Security Council ever since he took up his post. As our presidency continues, I am delighted to be upholding a longstanding tradition You've given us an edifying overview of the situation at the agency and its priorities. I would like to make the following remarks. The Security Council is duty-bound to address threats and breaches of international peace and security. That means crises and conflicts which are at the origin of this forced displacement. Seven out of 10 refugees falling within the agency's mandate come from just six states, most of which are on the Security Council's agenda. First and foremost, Sudan, where violence being waged despite the rules of law, has resulted in 2.8 million refugees on top of 9 million IDPs. We shouldn't let the agency address the humanitarian consequences on its own. France supports the work of the quintet. We call for the broadening and strengthening of the sanctions regime and the arms embargo. In Ukraine, a legal, brutal invasion, as well as the war being waged by Russia, has resulted in 10 million Ukrainians fleeing the country since 2022. In 2025, 117 million people have been compelled to flee, versus 65 million in 2015. In 10 years, the figure has almost doubled, which reflects a world confronted with conflicts, which are multiplying, becoming more protracted, and this is resulting in effects on food security, sanitation, and violations of international law. France welcomes the courage and the devotion of agency staff. It is incumbent upon the Council, much like other humanitarian actors, to ensure that they are given adequate protection as well as rapid, safe, and unfettered access. The Council has recalled in Resolution 2823 this responsibility to offer protection. Furthermore, it is our common duty to support host countries. Seventy percent of them are low and middle income countries. We need to help them better integrate refugees. It's a moral imperative, but also a matter of peace and security. Refugee returns have intensified over the last few years. We must provide assistance for these. Returns must be undertaken in conditions of dignity, safe and durable conditions. 1.8 million Syrians have gone back to their country since the Bashar al-Assad regime fell. They received the support of the Agency, and France is contributing to this effort. Aside from neighboring countries, which bear the brunt of the burden, Hosting and protecting refugees is a legal obligation, a universal one. France reiterates its commitment to the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, and we reiterate our trust in the agency as a guarantor for the convention's implementation. We call on all states who have not yet done so to ratify it. We support the reforms undertaken by the High Commissioner with a view to offering sustainable solutions to refugees and displaced persons. France remains committed to refugee inclusion. It's a longstanding commitment, and it's in keeping with our "avec elles, with them" multi-stakeholder pledge, launched in December 2023 at the Global Refugee Forum in the context of the Olympic and Paralympic Games in Paris. This initiative has paved the way for hundreds of projects helping women and girls refugees to become better integrated. We welcome the agency's aiming higher Education Initiative, which will be officially launched at the end of the year, the objective being to improve refugee access to higher education, the best way to give them professional opportunities and genuine economic empowerment. High Commissioner, we thank you for creating voluntary, safe and dignified conditions for refugee return. This is one of the key principles of international humanitarian law. Peace is our responsibility. I resume my function as President of the Security Council. There are no more names inscribed on the list of speakers. The meeting stands adjourned.
